title: Tithonus, husband of Dawn
greek: παρ᾽ ἀγαυοῦ Τιθωνοῖο (par' agauou Tithōnoio)
short: Tithonus was the Trojan prince whom Dawn (Eos) loved and carried off; she rises from his bed each morning.
body: The book opens with the same dawn formula as Iliad 11.1-2. Tithonus, a brother of Priam (Il. 20.237), was carried off by Eos for his beauty. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (218-38) tells the rest of the story: Dawn asked Zeus to make him immortal but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he aged endlessly and was shut away in a chamber, a voice without strength. The allusion is apt at the head of this book. Book V is built round Calypso's offer to make Odysseus 'immortal and ageless' (5.136), and Calypso herself cites Dawn's love for a mortal, Orion, as an example of the gods' jealousy (5.121-4). Tithonus is the mythical warning of what goddess-and-mortal unions can cost. Merry explains him simply as a youthful hero whom Eos carried off for his beauty; the Hymn's version is the fullest ancient account.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.1

title: The second council of the gods
greek: θεοὶ δὲ θόωκόνδε καθῖζον (theoi de thoōkonde kathizon)
short: A second assembly of the gods restarts the story of Odysseus, which has been left aside since Book I while Telemachus travelled.
body: Books I-IV followed Telemachus; Book V turns back to Odysseus with a council that repeats the situation of the first one (1.26-95), where Athena had already asked Zeus to free him and Zeus had agreed to send Hermes. Athena's complaint here is pieced together from lines used elsewhere: 5.8-12 repeat Mentor's words in the Ithacan assembly (2.230-4), and 5.14-17 repeat Menelaus' report of Proteus (4.557-60). Earlier analytic critics took the doublet as a sign that two versions of the poem had been joined. Modern commentators generally prefer to see a narrative device (Hainsworth's commentary is the place to follow the debate): Homer cannot easily tell two simultaneous stories, so he returns to the divine plan to mark the change of thread. Zeus's sharp reply ('Didst thou not thyself devise this plan?') points back to the first council and forward to the revenge.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.1-42

title: Scheria, land of the Phaeacians
greek: Σχερίην ἐρίβωλον (Scheriēn eribōlon)
short: Scheria is the island of the Phaeacians, the last stop of Odysseus' wanderings, half in the real world and half in fairyland.
body: Scheria is named here for the first time, in Zeus's summary of the plot: Odysseus will reach it on a raft on the twentieth day, be honoured 'as if he were a god', and be sent home with more treasure than he won at Troy (5.36-40). The name's origin is uncertain; ancient and modern guesses connect it with a word for 'mainland' or 'shore', but none is secure. From the fifth century BC the Corcyreans (Corfu) claimed it as their island and the Phaeacians as their ancestors (Thucydides 1.25.4), and the identification has remained popular. Within the poem, however, Scheria lies 'far off in the surging sea, the furthermost of men' (6.204-5), between the fabulous world of the Wanderings and the real Ithaca, and its people carry Odysseus across that border while he sleeps (13.70-92). 'Deep-soiled' (eribōlos) is a standard epithet of fertile land, appropriate to the orchards of Book VII.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.34

anchor: near of kin to the gods
title: The Phaeacians, 'near to the gods'
greek: Φαιήκων ἐς γαῖαν, οἳ ἀγχίθεοι γεγάασιν (Phaiēkōn es gaian, hoi ankhitheoi gegaasin)
short: The Phaeacians are called ankhitheoi, 'close to the gods', by descent from Poseidon and in their easy dealings with the immortals.
body: The adjective ankhitheos occurs only twice in Homer, here and at 19.279, both times of the Phaeacians. It has two senses that the poem keeps together: kinship (their king Nausithous was a son of Poseidon, 7.56-62) and closeness of contact (the gods feast openly among them, 7.201-6). Alcinous himself says they are near kin to the gods 'as are the Cyclopes and the wild tribes of the Giants' (7.205-6), an unsettling company, since both are emblems of lawless strength. The Phaeacians are the opposite of the Cyclopes they once lived beside (6.4-6): civilised, hospitable, sea-going. Yet their nearness to the gods is fragile. Poseidon resents their gift of safe convoy to all men (8.564-71) and punishes them after they take Odysseus home (13.125-87). The word thus prepares the ambiguous status of Scheria, a privileged but vulnerable society.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.35

title: Hermes' sandals and wand
greek: εἵλετο δὲ ῥάβδον, τῇ τ᾽ ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει (heileto de rhabdon, tēi t' andrōn ommata thelgei)
short: Hermes' golden sandals carry him over sea and land; his wand (rhabdos) charms men's eyes to sleep or wakes them.
body: The lines on Hermes' sandals and wand (5.44-8) are repeated word for word from Iliad 24.340-4, where Hermes sets out to guide Priam to Akhilleus. The repetition is typical of Homeric type-scenes (here, 'a god arms for a journey'), but it also carries meaning: in both poems Hermes is the god who crosses boundaries and conducts travellers through danger. The verb thelgei, 'charms, enchants', is the word used for magical spells and for the spell of song. The wand reappears at the opening of Book XXIV (24.1-5), where Hermes uses it to herd the suitors' souls to Hades; it is the ancestor of the later caduceus. Merry, in his note on 7.138, reports Nitzsch's view that the wand is not the symbol of natural sleep but of some extraordinary trance, and that Hermes as a dream-god belongs to a later conception of his office as guide of souls.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.138

title: Pieria
greek: Πιερίην (Pieriēn)
short: Pieria is the region north of Mount Olympus in Macedonia, the first stepping-stone of Hermes' flight from Olympus to the sea.
body: Hermes leaves Olympus, touches down in Pieria at the mountain's northern foot, and then skims the sea. Hera takes the same route at Iliad 14.225-7, stepping from Olympus to Pieria and Emathia on her way to Lemnos, so this is a fixed itinerary for gods descending to the Aegean. Pieria was also the birthplace of the Muses in Hesiod (Theogony 53-4), which is why later poets call them Pierides. In this book the detail does geographical work: it marks the immense distance between the gods' home and Calypso's island, which Hermes stresses in his grumble about the long salt journey with no cities or sacrifices on the way (5.100-2).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.50

title: Hermes like a sea-bird
greek: λάρῳ ὄρνιθι ἐοικώς (larōi ornithi eoikōs)
short: Hermes skims the waves like a sea-bird hunting fish; Murray's 'cormorant' renders laros, more probably a gull or tern.
body: Gods in Homer often move or disguise themselves 'like' birds, and it is debated whether such comparisons describe appearance, speed or an actual transformation. Here the bird is a laros, which LSJ glosses as a gull or other ravenous sea-bird. Merry notes that it may be the gull or the tern, neither of which dives deep, so Murray's 'cormorant' (a diving bird) is a free choice. The simile is unusually detailed: the bird hunts fish over the 'dread gulfs of the unresting sea' and wets its thick plumage in the brine. Its sea-world details prepare for the sea-birds round Calypso's cave (5.65-7) and for Ino, who rises from the deep 'like a sea-mew' (aithuiēi, 5.337). The sea, which will nearly kill Odysseus later in the book, is for the god a playground.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.51

title: Calypso's cave: the ideal landscape
greek: ὕλη δὲ σπέος ἀμφὶ πεφύκει τηλεθόωσα (hulē de speos amphi pephukei tēlethoōsa)
short: The description of Calypso's cave is the first great 'pleasant place' (locus amoenus) in European literature, so lovely that even a god stops to marvel.
body: The scene is seen through Hermes' eyes: fire of cedar and juniper, Calypso singing at her loom with a golden shuttle (like Circe at 10.221-3), a wood of alder, poplar and cypress, nesting birds, a vine, four springs, and meadows of violet and parsley (selinon, wild celery). Merry notes that the 'violet' (ion) is the ordinary blue scented violet. The passage became the model for countless later ideal landscapes, from Theocritus and Virgil to the gardens of Renaissance epic. But beauty here is also enclosure. Calypso's name suggests kaluptein, 'to cover, hide', and her island is 'the navel of the sea' (1.50), where Odysseus is held 'perforce'. The garden that delights the god is a prison to the man weeping on the shore (5.81-4). Compare the cultivated, communal orchard of Alcinous (7.112-32).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.72
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.63-74

title: The gods' jealousy (zēlēmones)
greek: σχέτλιοί ἐστε, θεοί, ζηλήμονες ἔξοχον ἄλλων (schetlioi este, theoi, zēlēmones exochon allōn)
short: Calypso accuses the male gods of a double standard: they begrudge goddesses the mortal lovers they freely take themselves.
body: Zēlēmōn, 'jealous, grudging', occurs only here in Homer. Merry records an ancient variant, dēlēmones, 'harmful', but the context of sexual jealousy favours zēlēmones. Calypso's speech (5.118-44) is a small catalogue of precedents in the form of a complaint: Dawn and Orion, Demeter and Iasion, each ending in the mortal's death at a god's hand. The point is clear: male gods lie with mortal women constantly (Zeus lists his own affairs at Il. 14.315-28), but a goddess's open union with a man is punished. Her protest gives Calypso dignity and a voice of her own in a scene that could have been simple obedience; she yields, but on her own terms, claiming that she will help him 'with a ready heart' and denying that the plan to send him was hers; Odysseus later tells Arete he could not tell whether a message from Zeus or her own change of mind made her let him go (7.262-3).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.118

title: Orion and Ortygia
greek: Ὠρίων (Ōriōn); ἐν Ὀρτυγίῃ (en Ortugiēi)
short: Orion, the giant hunter loved by Dawn, was killed by Artemis on Ortygia, Calypso's first example of the gods' jealousy.
body: Orion is in Homer both a hunter and a constellation: Odysseus sees his shade hunting in the Underworld (11.572-5), and later in this same book he steers by the Bear 'which watches Orion' (5.274). Here Dawn's love for him is cut short when Artemis shoots him with her 'gentle shafts', the Homeric phrase for sudden, painless death. Later writers give other causes (an assault on Artemis or on one of her companions), but Homer only implies divine resentment. Ortygia, 'Quail Island', is the name of more than one place: ancient sources apply it to Delos (or an islet beside it) and to the island at the heart of Syracuse. Merry suggests that Syracusan colonists carried the cult of Delian Artemis, and the name, to their new home; Artemis' connection makes the Delian Ortygia the likelier sense here.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.121-4
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.121-4

title: Iasion and Demeter
greek: Ἰασίωνι (Iasiōni) ... νειῷ ἔνι τριπόλῳ (neiōi eni tripolōi)
short: Demeter lay with the mortal Iasion in a 'thrice-ploughed fallow'; Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt, Calypso's second example.
body: Hesiod tells the same story more fully: Demeter lay with Iasion 'in a thrice-ploughed fallow in the rich land of Crete' and bore Plutus, Wealth (Theogony 969-74). The thrice-ploughed field is significant. Fallow land was ploughed several times before sowing, and a union of the corn-goddess with a mortal in such a field has long been read as reflecting a fertility rite of ritual intercourse in the furrow; Merry also reports the suggestion that Iasion's name is connected with the earth. Homer gives the punishment, not the offspring: Zeus 'was not long without knowledge' and struck Iasion down. As with Orion, the mortal pays for the goddess's love, which is exactly what Calypso fears the gods intend in demanding Odysseus' release, though in his case it is the goddess who loses.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.125

title: Immortal and ageless: Odysseus' choice
greek: θήσειν ἀθάνατον καὶ ἀγήραον ἤματα πάντα (thēsein athanaton kai agēraon ēmata panta)
short: Calypso offered Odysseus immortality and eternal youth; he chose instead mortal life, home and Penelope.
body: The phrase 'immortal and ageless all his days' is the full formula for divine existence; it is used of Hephaestus' golden dogs at 7.94, and Odysseus repeats Calypso's offer to Arete (7.256-8) and later to Penelope (23.335-7). Its significance is best seen against Tithonus, mentioned in the first line of the book, who was given immortality without agelessness. To refuse such an offer is an extraordinary assertion of human values: Odysseus prefers a life bounded by death but filled with identity, family and fame. Calypso's name and island imply concealment; to stay would be to disappear from the human world and from song. Many critics see this as the poem's defining moral choice, the Odyssean counterpart to Akhilleus' choice between long life and glory (Il. 9.410-16).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.136

title: Odysseus on Calypso's shore
greek: παρ᾽ οὐκ ἐθέλων ἐθελούσῃ (par' ouk ethelōn etheloushēi)
short: Odysseus sleeps with Calypso by compulsion, 'unwilling beside the willing'; by day he weeps on the shore, longing for home.
body: The first sight of the hero of the Odyssey is of a man in tears. The Greek plays the participles against each other, ouk ethelōn ethelousēi, a polyptoton that sets refusal against desire in a single line. His 'sweet life was ebbing away' (5.152-3) as he mourned for his nostos, the return home that is the poem's central theme; the word nostos is used here (5.153). The phrase 'the nymph was no longer pleasing' (5.153) suggests that this was not always so; seven years have passed (7.259). Hermes, arriving, does not even find him in the cave (5.81-4). The passage establishes the fundamental choice of the book: the comfort and immortality offered by Calypso against the hardship, mortality and identity of Ithaca.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.151-8

anchor: the down-flowing water of the Styx
title: The oath by the Styx
greek: τὸ κατειβόμενον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ (to kateibomenon Stugos hudōr)
short: The oath by the river Styx, the boundary of the Underworld, was the most binding oath a god could swear.
body: Odysseus will not set out until Calypso swears to plot no further harm. She swears by earth, heaven and Styx, in lines identical to Hera's oath at Iliad 15.36-8. Hesiod explains why the oath is so dreadful: a god who forswears it lies breathless for a year, without nectar or ambrosia, and is then excluded from the gods' councils and feasts for nine more years (Theogony 775-806). Merry summarises this tradition in his note. Odysseus' suspicion is itself characteristic. Calypso smiles and calls him a 'knave' (alitrós), 'not stunted in wit' (5.182-3), a goddess's affectionate recognition of his mētis, the cunning intelligence that defines him. Circe is made to swear the same oath before he will share her bed (10.343-5).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.185

anchor: such sort as mortal men eat
title: Mortal food and ambrosia
greek: οἷα βροτοὶ ἄνδρες ἔδουσιν (hoia brotoi andres edousin)
short: At their last meal Odysseus eats mortal food while Calypso eats ambrosia and nectar: the table itself shows the gulf between them.
body: Homer marks the difference between gods and men by what they eat. Gods take ambrosia and nectar and have ichor, not blood, because they 'eat no bread' (Il. 5.341-2); men are 'eaters of bread'. When Calypso fed Hermes she set out ambrosia (5.93), but for Odysseus she lays 'all manner of food ... such as mortal men eat', while her maids serve her divine fare. Odysseus even sits on the chair Hermes has just left, an exact staging of the contrast. The scene quietly enacts the choice he is about to state: had he accepted immortality, he would have shared her food. Food and the belly remain a marker of human limitation throughout the poem (7.215-21).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.196-9

title: Penelope and Calypso compared
greek: περίφρων Πηνελόπεια (periphrōn Pēnelopeia)
short: Odysseus tactfully concedes that Penelope is inferior to Calypso in beauty, yet insists that he longs to go home.
body: Calypso's last appeal (5.203-13) turns on comparison: she is not inferior to his wife 'in form or stature'. Odysseus answers with diplomatic skill. He grants everything she says about beauty and mortality, which a goddess cannot be contradicted on, and then states his wish without argument: 'even so I wish and long day by day to reach my home'. Penelope's standing epithet, periphrōn, 'very thoughtful, prudent', hints at what Calypso cannot offer, a partner of equal mind; the poem will later celebrate their 'like-mindedness' (homophrosynē, 6.181-5) and the test of the bed in Book XXIII. His readiness to endure further suffering, 'I will endure it, having in my breast a heart that endures affliction' (5.222), restates the epithet polutlas, 'much-enduring', that the poem gives him.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.215-24

title: The building of the raft
greek: σχεδίη (schediē); ἐείκοσι δ᾽ ἔκβαλε πάντα (eeikosi d' ekbale panta)
short: Odysseus builds his vessel himself, with Calypso's tools; the passage is the most detailed account of shipbuilding in Homer.
body: Calypso calls it a schediē, a 'raft', and Murray follows her. But the technical terms describe something more like a boat: timbers smoothed 'straight to the line', bored and joined with pegs (gomphoi, which Merry glosses as shipwrights' 'trenails') and joints (harmoniai), shaped as wide as a carpenter marks the hull of a broad merchant ship, with decking (ikria) on close-set ribs, gunwales, a mast with yard, a steering oar and a wattle fence against the waves. Lionel Casson argued that Homer is describing the mortise-and-tenon technique of ancient hull construction, so that the 'raft' is in effect a small ship. Thematically, the scene shows Odysseus as a skilled craftsman, as with the bed he built round an olive trunk (23.189-201), and it takes four days of labour on a rigid timetable.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.243-61
L. Casson, 'Odysseus' Boat', American Journal of Philology 85 (1964) 61-4
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.228-61

title: Steering by the stars
greek: Πληιάδας ... ὀψὲ δύοντα Βοώτην, Ἄρκτον θ᾽ (Plēiadas ... opse duonta Boōtēn, Arkton th')
short: Odysseus navigates by night, watching the Pleiades, Bootes and the Bear, keeping the Bear on his left as Calypso instructed.
body: This is Homer's only description of celestial navigation. The Pleiades, Bootes ('the ploughman', which 'sets late' because it lies along the horizon as it sinks) and the Great Bear or Wain are the constellations a Greek sailor would know; Hesiod uses the Pleiades to time ploughing and sailing (Works and Days 383-4, 619-21). Lines 5.273-5 repeat the description of the stars on Akhilleus' shield (Il. 18.487-9): the Bear 'circles where it is and watches Orion, and alone has no part in the baths of Ocean', that is, it never sets below the horizon at Greek latitudes. Merry notes that ancient critics objected that other northern stars also never set. Keeping the Bear on the left means sailing east, so Calypso's island lies in the far west. The voyage takes seventeen days.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.272-5

title: Poseidon's return from the Solymi
greek: ἐκ Σολύμων ὀρέων (ek Solumōn oreōn)
short: Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, sees Odysseus from the mountains of the Solymi, a people of south-western Asia Minor.
body: Poseidon's absence among the Ethiopians was what allowed the gods to plan Odysseus' release in Book I (1.22-6); now he is coming back, and the plan meets its obstacle. The Solymi were a warlike people of the Lycian region; Bellerophon fought them (Il. 6.184-5, 6.203-4). Merry places their mountains in the Taurus range and observes that Homer seems to distinguish the Solymi from the Lycians. The geography is vague in a way typical of gods' journeys, but the view is enormous: from southern Asia Minor Poseidon sees a raft somewhere in the western sea. His soliloquy ('Out on it!', 5.286-90) is a counterpart to Zeus's council, a single god's anger against the collective will.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.283
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.282-3

title: 'His knees were loosened': the hero's monologue
greek: καὶ τότ᾽ Ὀδυσσῆος λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ (kai tot' Odussēos luto gounata kai philon ētor)
short: A fixed formula for despair introduces the first of Odysseus' four monologues in the storm, each spoken 'to his own mighty spirit'.
body: 'His knees and his heart were loosened' is a formula for the collapse of strength in fear or exhaustion; in the Iliad 'loosening the knees' is often a phrase for killing. The next line, 'deeply moved he spoke to his own mighty spirit' (pros hon megalētora thumon), introduces a deliberative monologue, a type found in the Iliad when a warrior stands alone in danger (Odysseus himself at Il. 11.403-10, Hector at 22.98-130). In Book V the type is used four times (5.299, 5.355, 5.407, 5.465), and the formulas recur at 5.406 and 5.464. The repetitions are structural: each crisis brings a pause in which Odysseus weighs options and chooses the safer course. The hero of the Odyssey is thus defined by deliberation under pressure as much as by action.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.297-312

title: 'Thrice blessed those who died at Troy'
greek: τρισμάκαρες Δαναοὶ καὶ τετράκις (trismakares Danaoi kai tetrakis)
short: Facing a nameless death at sea, Odysseus envies the Greeks who fell at Troy and received burial and fame; Virgil's Aeneas echoes him.
body: Death at sea was the worst of deaths for a Greek, because it left no body, no funeral and no tomb, and so no lasting memorial. Odysseus wishes he had died in the fight over Akhilleus' corpse (described at 24.36-42), when he would have received funeral rites (kterea) and the Achaeans would have spread his kleos, his fame. The passage measures the Odyssey's values against the Iliad's: glory belongs to those who die in battle, but this hero's story requires survival. Virgil imitates the passage at the first appearance of Aeneas, also in a storm: 'o terque quaterque beati' (Aeneid 1.94-101), with Aeneas recalling Hector and Sarpedon. The variation 'three times, aye four times' became proverbial in Latin.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.306-12

anchor: the North Wind bears the thistle-tufts
title: The thistle-tuft simile
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ὀπωρινὸς Βορέης φορέῃσιν ἀκάνθας (hōs d' hot' opōrinos Boreēs phoreēisin akanthas)
short: The raft is tossed like thistle-down blown across the plain in autumn, and the four winds pass it from one to another like a ball.
body: Two images combine. The first is a farm-world simile: dry thistle-heads, matted together, blown over a field by the autumn north wind, a picture of something light, helpless and directionless. The second turns the four winds into players tossing the raft between them, a game whose plaything is a man's life. Homeric similes often take their material from the ordinary world of farm, weather and craft, and the contrast with the terrifying scene is part of their effect. Here the triviality of thistle-down makes the raft's helplessness vivid. The winds named (Notos, Boreas, Euros, Zephyros) are the full four that Poseidon unleashed at 5.295-6.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.328-32

title: Ino-Leucothea
greek: Κάδμου θυγάτηρ, καλλίσφυρος Ἰνώ, Λευκοθέη (Kadmou thugatēr, kallisphuros Inō, Leukotheē)
short: Ino, daughter of Cadmus of Thebes, was once a mortal; after leaping into the sea she became the sea-goddess Leucothea, 'the White Goddess'.
body: Homer says only that she was once a mortal 'of human speech' and now has honour among the gods in the sea. Later sources tell the story: Ino, persecuted by Hera (or fleeing her maddened husband Athamas), leapt into the sea with her son Melicertes, and both were made sea-deities, she as Leucothea, he as Palaemon. Merry gives this account and notes that she was honoured as a goddess. She is a fitting rescuer for Odysseus: a former mortal who passed through the sea into a new life, she offers a man near death a means of passing through it himself. She appears 'like a sea-mew' (aithuia, a diving bird), the last of the book's sea-bird comparisons, and she is the one deity in the storm who acts from pity (5.336).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.333

title: Ino's veil (krēdemnon)
greek: τῆ δέ, τόδε κρήδεμνον ὑπὸ στέρνοιο τανύσσαι (tē de, tode krēdemnon hupo sternoio tanussai)
short: Ino gives Odysseus her immortal veil to tie under his chest; it will keep him from drowning, but he must throw it back into the sea.
body: A krēdemnon is a woman's head-covering, the veil that Penelope holds before her face (1.334) and that Andromache throws off in grief (Il. 22.470). The word is also used metaphorically of a city's battlements, Troy's 'holy krēdemna' (Il. 16.100). Its use here as a life-preserver is magical: Merry notes that it was to be tied 'under the breast' as a sort of lifebelt. Ino's conditions follow a folk-tale pattern: the magic object must be returned and the recipient must turn away, a gesture of respect toward the powers below. Odysseus obeys at 5.459-62, and the river carries the veil back to her hands. David West has argued that the veil identifies Odysseus with Penelope and signifies the recovery of chastity and, ultimately, of the marriage, which suggests why it shields him here. His distrust of the gift (5.356-64) is typically cautious.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.346
D. West, 'Shipwrecked Spouses: Leukothea's Veil and Marital Reunion in The Odyssey', New England Classical Journal 47.2 (2020) 1-14

title: The raft scattered like chaff; riding a plank
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ἄνεμος ζαὴς ἠΐων θημῶνα τινάξῃ (hōs d' anemos zaēs ēiōn thēmōna tinaxēi)
short: The raft Odysseus built so carefully is scattered like a heap of dry straw; he bestrides a single beam 'as though riding a horse'.
body: The second agricultural simile of the storm repeats the idea of the thistle-tufts but with a sharper edge: the craftsmanship of 5.243-61 is undone in an instant, and the timbers scatter like chaff from the threshing floor. Then comes an extraordinary image of the hero 'riding a plank like a horse' (kelēth' hōs hippon elaunōn). The phrase anticipates the poem's metaphor of ships as 'horses of the sea' (4.708). Only now, stripped of Calypso's clothes, does he trust himself to Ino's veil. Nakedness is significant: he arrives in Scheria with nothing at all, and his identity will have to be rebuilt from nothing among the Phaeacians.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.368-71

title: Aegae, Poseidon's home
greek: ἵκετ᾽ ἐς Αἰγάς, ὅθι οἱ κλυτὰ δώματ᾽ ἔασιν (iket' es Aigas, hothi hoi kluta dōmat' easin)
short: Aegae was Poseidon's cult centre and underwater palace; having done his worst, he drives off home, and Athena takes over.
body: At Iliad 13.17-31 Poseidon steps from Samothrace to Aegae, where his golden palace lies in the depths of the sea, and drives his chariot over the waves. Ancient scholars disagreed over the location. Merry records two views: a town on the coast of Achaea in the northern Peloponnese, where Poseidon was worshipped (cf. Il. 8.203), or a submerged rock or islet; he adds that the word itself suggests waves and storm (aiges, 'waves', in later Greek). Poseidon's departure is decisive. Athena 'took other counsel', a formula marking a change of plan, and stills every wind except the north wind that carries Odysseus to Scheria (5.382-7). In Book VI she will tell us why she has not acted openly before: she would not oppose her uncle (6.329-31).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.381
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.381

title: The father restored to his children (a 'reverse simile')
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἀσπάσιος βίοτος παίδεσσι φανήῃ / πατρός (hōs d' hot' an aspasios biotos paidessi phanēēi / patros)
short: The sight of land is as welcome to Odysseus as a father's recovery from wasting illness is to his children.
body: The simile inverts the actual situation: Odysseus is himself a father whose life is endangered and whose son longs for his return, yet here he is compared to the children and the land to the restored father. Helene Foley called such comparisons, where a character is likened to someone of the opposite position or role, 'reverse similes', and showed that the Odyssey uses them systematically to suggest the disruption and restoration of social order. The most famous reverse simile, at the reunion of husband and wife, takes up this very scene: Penelope welcomes Odysseus as shipwrecked sailors welcome land (23.233-40). Merry notes that the verb phainesthai, 'to appear', is used of the reappearance of what was thought lost.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.394-7
H. P. Foley, 'Reverse Similes and Sex Roles in the Odyssey', Arethusa 11 (1978) 7-26

title: The octopus simile
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε πουλύποδος θαλάμης ἐξελκομένοιο (hōs d' hote poulupodos thalamēs exelkomenoio)
short: Torn from the rocks, Odysseus leaves skin on the stone as an octopus pulled from its hole carries pebbles on its suckers.
body: Murray's 'cuttlefish' renders poulupous, literally 'many-foot', the octopus. The point of comparison is reversed in a characteristic way: the pebbles cling to the octopus as it is dragged from its lair, while it is Odysseus' skin that is torn off and left on the rock (5.434-5). The precise observation suggests familiarity with fishing on Aegean coasts. The octopus was also an emblem of cunning adaptability in Greek thought (later proverbs urged one to have 'the mind of an octopus', changing colour with circumstances), so some critics see an apt hint at the many-minded hero, though the simile itself stresses only his clinging grip and its painful price. Athena twice intervenes here, putting a thought in his mind and granting prudence (5.427, 5.437), lest he perish 'beyond his fate' (huper moron, 5.436).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.432-5

title: Odysseus supplicates the river
greek: ἱκέτης δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι (hiketēs de toi eukhomai einai)
short: Odysseus prays to the unknown river-god as a suppliant (hiketēs), and the god stills his current to let him land.
body: Supplication (hikesia) is one of the institutions that structure the Phaeacian books. A suppliant, by a formal gesture and appeal, placed himself under the protection of the person addressed and of Zeus. Odysseus does not know the river's name ('whosoever thou art') but uses the language of the ritual: he has come 'to thy stream and to thy knees', and a wanderer is 'reverend' (aidoios) even to the gods. The prayer is answered at once. This is the first of a sequence of supplications: to Nausicaa, at a distance (6.141-85), and to Arete at the hearth (7.142-54). John Gould's classic study of hikesia analyses the gestures, such as clasping knees, and the obligations they created; Odysseus' handling of them in Books VI-VII is a demonstration of social skill.

sources.cite: J. Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973) 74-103

title: The two bushes: wild and cultivated olive
greek: τὸν μὲν φυλίης, τὸν δ᾽ ἐλαίης (ton men phuliēs, ton d' elaiēs)
short: Odysseus shelters under two bushes growing from one root; phulia is probably the wild olive, elaia the cultivated one.
body: Murray's 'thorn' reflects an older interpretation. Merry notes that phulia is 'generally and best taken' as the wild olive, though some thought it an evergreen thorn. Read that way, the two intertwined bushes, wild and tame olive from a single stem, have invited symbolic interpretation: Odysseus, between the wild world of the Wanderings and the civilised world he is entering, sleeps where nature and culture grow together. The olive is Athena's tree, and it marks his arrival at home too, for Odysseus and Athena sit beside the trunk of the sacred olive in Ithaca to plan the suitors' destruction (13.372-3) and his marriage-bed is built round an olive trunk (23.190-204). The shelter, proof against wind, sun and rain, is described in lines that resemble the boar's lair at 19.440-3, where Odysseus got his scar.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.477

title: The brand hidden in the ashes
greek: σπέρμα πυρὸς σῴζων (sperma puros sōizōn)
short: Odysseus buries himself in leaves as a lonely farmer buries a live brand in the embers to save a 'seed of fire' for the morning.
body: The book ends with one of Homer's most quiet and suggestive similes. A man on a remote farm, with no neighbour from whom to borrow a light, keeps a brand smouldering under ash overnight. Merry spells out the comparison: Odysseus keeps his spark of life alive under a covering of leaves. The isolation is part of the point. Like the farmer 'who has no neighbours', Odysseus has no companions, ship or possessions left; all that remains is the bare life in him, which must be preserved until it can be rekindled among the Phaeacians. Athena's gift of sleep closes the book, as sleep will mark the transitions at the end of Books VI-VIII and the voyage home in Book XIII.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 5.488
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 5.488-91
